subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: From a rectangular sheet of dimensions 30 cm × 80 cm, four equal squares of side x cm are removed at the corners, and the sides are then turned up so as to form an open rectangular box. Find the value of x so that the volume of the box is the greatest.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what the three dimensions of the box are in terms of x, what range x can take, and what you do with the second root.

steps.label: Write the volume in x
steps.margin_note: First mark. The examiner looks for the two bracket factors 30 − 2x and 80 − 2x with height x. Write the domain 0 < x < 15 on the same line — the rejection later depends on it.

recall.must_convey: That the box measures x by (30 − 2x) by (80 − 2x), so V = x(30 − 2x)(80 − 2x), with 0 < x < 15.

steps.why: The cut removes x from each end of every side, so each dimension loses 2x, not x. Writing the domain now is what turns the rejection in step 3 into a reasoned move rather than a guess.
common_mistakes: Subtracting x instead of 2x from each side of the sheet.
Leaving the domain unwritten, so the root x = 30 cannot be rejected with a reason.
Forgetting that x itself is the height of the box.
steps.memory_tip: Each side loses a square at both ends, so subtract 2x. The shorter side 30 sets the limit, which is why x must stay below 15.

steps.label: Differentiate and solve V′(x) = 0
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Expand before differentiating — the product rule on three factors is easy to get wrong. Take the factor 4 out of V′ before using the quadratic formula.

recall.must_convey: That V′(x) = 4(3x² − 110x + 600) and solving it gives x = 30 and x = 20/3.
accept: expand first and then differentiate the cubic

the two roots are thirty and twenty by three

steps.why: Expanding first turns a triple product into an ordinary cubic, so one differentiation gives a quadratic that the standard formula solves. The common factor 4 comes out to keep the numbers small.
common_mistakes: Applying the product rule to three factors and dropping one term.
Dividing V′ by 4 but forgetting to divide the 2400 as well.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply out before you differentiate. A cubic in one line is faster and safer than a product rule over three brackets.

steps.label: Reject the root outside the domain
steps.margin_note: Third mark, and it is a real mark, not a formality. The examiner looks for the reason, not just the word rejected — say which dimension turns negative.
lines: The domain found in step 1 is 0 < x < 15,
so test both roots against it.

lines: If x = 30, then the breadth is 30 − 2(30) = −30 cm,
a negative length. No box exists, so this root is rejected.

recall.must_convey: That x = 30 is rejected because it makes the breadth 30 − 2x negative, leaving x = 20/3 as the only usable root.

steps.why: Calculus finds every stationary point of the algebraic formula, including ones the physical situation does not allow. Naming the dimension that turns negative is what shows the rejection is reasoned.
common_mistakes: Rejecting x = 30 with no reason written down.
Choosing the larger root because larger x looks like a larger box.
steps.memory_tip: Test every root against the domain you wrote in step 1. A root that makes any side negative describes no box.

steps.why: Setting V′ to zero only locates where the volume stops changing. The sign of V″ is what proves this point is the greatest volume and not the least, so it is a step in its own right.
common_mistakes: Stopping at x = 20/3 with no second derivative test.
Writing x = 6.67 as the exact answer instead of the fraction 20/3.
steps.memory_tip: Second derivative negative means the graph bends downward there, so the stationary point is a local maximum; on 0 < x < 15 it gives the greatest volume.

insider_note: Each side loses 2x, not x, because a square is cut at BOTH ends. The domain 0 < x < 15 comes from the shorter side, and roots outside it are rejected.
